book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons

chapters.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md
ch06 - Part Five D Is for Destiny.md
chapters.relation: This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.

chapters.file: ch07 - PART ONE - F IS FOR FORTUNE.md

chapters.relation: Richard Davies uses Aristotle's Poetics (the principles of closure, relevance, and the unities of place and time) to defend Lost's tangled narrative as an epic rather than a broken tragedy, arguing that flashbacks, flash-forwards like Jack's 'We have to go back,' and multi-season arcs such as Juliet's remain within Aristotelian bounds. He then imports McTaggart's contrast between eternalism and presentism to explain why a flash-forward is philosophically unsettling, and argues that changing the past (as season 5's time travel invites) generates a logical contradiction from which anything follows, so viewers must 'shield' Hurley's 1977 experiences to keep enjoying the plot.

chapters.file: ch09 - None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It.md
chapters.relation: William J. Devlin applies David Lewis's distinction between external time and the traveler's personal time to Lost's season 5-6 time jumps, showing how Faraday's eternalist 'whatever happened, happened' (Chang's unbreakable rules) contrasts with the branching-universe model that Faraday later embraces with 'we're the variables.' Lewis's account resolves specific puzzles: why baby Miles and adult Miles can coexist without violating the indiscernibility of identicals, whether Faraday could kill his mother Eloise (the grandfather paradox), and the uncaused causal loop of the compass Locke and Richard pass between 1954 and 2007.

Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'

Deborah R. Barnbaum reads season 6's flash-sideways as a set of counterfactual conditionals ('if Sawyer weren't a con man, then he would have been a cop') and uses David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics and his ordered similarity priorities to judge which are plausible. She argues Sawyer-as-cop is a 'closest world' change of one fact while Jack-and-Juliet-with-a-son changes too much to be true, and she pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance and A Theory of Justice as a parallel counterfactual thought experiment governing how the castaways should ration scarce water and medicine.

chapters.file: ch12 - PART TWO - O IS FOR ORIGIN.md

chapters.relation: Charles Taliaferro and Dan Kastrul argue, following Aristotle's dispositional account of character, that who the castaways are is a matter of what they would do under different conditions, illustrated by Mr. Eko's circumstance-driven violence and Ben Linus's shifting good-guy/bad-guy conduct. They deploy Plato's Myth of Gyges (the ring of invisibility) to test whether characters like Sun would act justly only when watched, and, against a completely reversed morality ('an island where skinning babies is good'), they argue via Chesterton that some overriding values are non-relative, so the show never fully reverses good and evil even amid its mysteries.

Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.

Jeremy Barris argues that Lost dramatizes the structure of life itself, using Heidegger's claim that the inquirer's own being is the clue to all questions and his notion of 'thrownness' to read the castaways' accidental arrival as a mirror of our own bewildering birth into circumstances we did not make. He reframes the show's central puzzle as 'the question of life after birth,' contends against Sartre and Camus that life is neither fully sensible nor fully absurd but a half-understood riddle, and invokes Wittgenstein's On Certainty to show that total doubt is impossible because understanding senselessness presupposes understanding something.

Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.

chapters.file: ch17 - PART THREE - U IS FOR UNITY.md

chapters.relation: Richard Davies analyzes the post-crash survivors as living in a genuine 'state of nature' and grades its severity by how scarce the contested good is (the water shortage as a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers versus Sawyer's 'possession is nine-tenths'). He compares Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau on human nature — labeling the poles 'Innocence' (Hurley, Rousseau, Hume) and 'Trust No 1' (Sawyer, Hobbes) — and uses the repeated prisoners' dilemma and the tit-for-tat strategy to argue that the castaways build a Lockean civil society by signaling through shared language and cooperating first, while the discovery of the Others (Ethan) triggers Hobbesian non-cooperation.

Peter S. Fosl argues that Lost pretends to a liberal social order — Jack rising by consent in a Lockean scheme of natural rights, Rousseau's general will ('live together, die alone'), and Hume's sympathy and pity binding the survivors — but that its treatment of the Others betrays a darker politics. Reading the survivor/Other conflict through Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy thesis (notably absent Hobbes), he contends the show, like post-9/11 America, needs an enemy to exterminate, and that the finale's Jacob/Man-in-Black war and Jack's Christlike sacrificial death repudiate the Kantian liberal ideal of persons as ends, resolving conflict through Schmittian and Christian redemptive violence instead.
